messages.subject: Bi-Factor Model Theory
parts:
Dear Phil,

This question is more theoretical in nature rather than related to R or the mirt package. Would be glad also to discuss this with the community.

Let's say that I have a sample of 500 respondents, based on balanced quota sampling, who provided their responses for a set of questionnaire items on a particular print advertisement that is shown to them. There are 5 groups of respondents and for each group, a different advertisement is shown. So, there are 5 advertisements that are used for the sample groups. The objective of the survey is to determine which advertisement has the greatest impact on influencing the buying decision (LikelyToBuy) among consumers. The survey questionnaire is consist of 22 items, each requiring the respondent to provide a rating of 1 (not agree at all) - 5 (agree totally).

Also, the 5 advertisements are from 5 different competing brands for the same product category.

The 22 items in the questionnaire can be easily grouped into concept related ideas: advertisement (e.g. attractive graphics, intereting copy, great headline, etc.), product (e.g. good quality, value for money, high performance, etc.) and brand (e.g. trustworthy, innovative, vibrant, etc.)

The approach to me seems clear - a Full-Information Item Bi-Factor Analysis and the function bfactor() in your mirt package is probably the only one in the entire realm of R that can do this for a multi-group situation (like the one stated above). I envision a General, g along side the specific factors of Advert, a, Product, p and Brand, b. Using bfactor(), convergence achieved successfully and I was able to obtain the necessary model parameters.

g - general attitude towards the brand
a - advert strength
p - product strength
b - specific attitude towards the brand

So here comes the theoretical part:

1. Is it valid, as a analysis procedure, to combine the responses from the different groups into one and perform a single MIRT to establish the latent dimensions of g, a, p and b which is then used as regression variables to predict the outcome variable of LikelyToBuy among the respondents? Ultimately, any significant differences among the respondent groups will then establish which advert is the superior one. In this approach, everyone is put on the same scale for each of the latent factor in consideration.

2. DIF - how should I consider this in the context of the above analysis? As mentioned above, the 5 respondent groups are sampled based on balance quota. Equal proportions of gender, age-group, race and location. So any possible existence of DIF would be from the different ads shown to the different groups. Does existence of DIF imply differences in the 'performance' of the ads?

The objective of the survey is to determine which advertisement has the greatest impact on influencing the buying decision (LikelyToBuy) among consumers. The survey questionnaire is consist of 22 items, each requiring the respondent to provide a rating of 1 (not agree at all) - 5 (agree totally).

Also, the 5 advertisements are from 5 different competing brands for the same product category.

The 22 items in the questionnaire can be easily grouped into concept related ideas: advertisement (e.g. attractive graphics, intereting copy, great headline, etc.), product (e.g. good quality, value for money, high performance, etc.) and brand (e.g. trustworthy, innovative, vibrant, etc.)

The approach to me seems clear - a Full-Information Item Bi-Factor Analysis and the function bfactor() in your mirt package is probably the only one in the entire realm of R that can do this for a multi-group situation (like the one stated above). I envision a General, g along side the specific factors of Advert, a, Product, p and Brand, b. Using bfactor(), convergence achieved successfully and I was able to obtain the necessary model parameters.

g - general attitude towards the brand
a - advert strength
p - product strength
b - specific attitude towards the brand

This sounds like a good approach to the problem. The emphases and power will come from whether there is no DIF in the items so that you can save some (5-1) * (22 + 44) = 264 degrees of freedom (instead of having 2 unified slopes across groups you would have 2 unique slopes for 5 groups, and so on). The key here would be to look at the latent mean/variance differences across groups for the g factor, holding the items constant (no DIF).

So here comes the theoretical part:

1. Is it valid, as a analysis procedure, to combine the responses from the different groups into one and perform a single MIRT to establish the latent dimensions of g, a, p and b which is then used as regression variables to predict the outcome variable of LikelyToBuy among the respondents? Ultimately, any significant differences among the respondent groups will then establish which advert is the superior one. In this approach, everyone is put on the same scale for each of the latent factor in consideration.

Given the outline of your study, I think this is reasonable at least at first, so long as you realize you are making a no DIF assumption. From a pragmatic point of view I think this is where you should start anyway since with N = 500 you are going to run out of df pretty quickly anyway. Again, the focus is on what happens when you free the latent means, and whether this improves the likelihood (hence indicates that latent group differences are present).

2. DIF - how should I consider this in the context of the above analysis? As mentioned above, the 5 respondent groups are sampled based on balance quota. Equal proportions of gender, age-group, race and location. So any possible existence of DIF would be from the different ads shown to the different groups. Does existence of DIF imply differences in the 'performance' of the ads?

Unfortunately unbalance quota is not what causes DIF, it's the properties within the populations themselves that cause it. For instance, in a psychopathology test for depression its well known that females have a uniform DIF effect in items that ask about 'crying'. The reason is because females, on average, simply tend to cry more, and responding highly on these items may not indicate a higher level of depression. The female participant have in factor have the same θ value as a male taking the same test, but just tend to answer in the upper extremes for these items. 

Notice, however, that regardless of the proportion of males and females there is this property remains, and therefore as little to do with the sampling method chosen. If you were trying to obtain test properties for the entire mixed population, ignoring specific person level attributes such as gender and race, then it would make more sense to randomly sample from this population directly rather than focus on a balanced quota design. This would allow you to make a more unbiased construction of a test, conditional on the entire population (and therefore, in general, applicable to all, but certainly not optimal for some specific subgroups; it may in fact be very wrong if the groups marginalized over are highly discrepant, but using this approach you should be able to find DIF for those groups fairly easily). 

Just a technical reminder as well: while bfactor() supports MG analysis, you should be careful in how it is set up since the specific factor latent means/variance cannot be freed. This is due to the method of integration which the function capitalizes on, a cost of which is a less flexible model. Not that this matters in this case really, and it's probably better that way anyway given the identification problems with freeing multiple latent parameters in multidimensional models. Cheers.

Phil
